Senses.Explanation: Who is the one who takes none of the myriad dharmas as companion? The question is Layman Pang Yun's own: he first asked Shitou — who is the one who takes none of the myriad dharmas as companion? — and Shitou covered his mouth; Pang had a stirring of insight, carried the same question to Mazu, and got the answer no one has improved on: when you can swallow all the water of the West River in one gulp, then I will tell you. The Empty Valley Collection raises the exchange with Touzi Qing's capping line — even the thousand sages do not know him — and Linquan's note: the mouth hard as iron, the heart softer than cotton; then retells the whole life, Xiangzhou's layman Pang Yun of Hengyang, courtesy name Daoxuan, sinking his fortune in the Xiang River and going begging with his wife in bamboo-woven baskets. Wuyi Yuanlai answers it himself in tea-talk verse: who is the one who takes none of the myriad dharmas as companion? In the red-dust heap, the whole body shows; knowing the myriad dharmas empty and thingless, what mountains and rivers could block the eye? — and piles on the three-year-old with a snow-white head and the stone tiger birthing young before the cliff. Ruibai Mingxue writes it to a dying patron as the thing to hold: look into who-is-the-one-who-takes-none-of-the-myriad-dharmas-as-companion, buckle it down with one buckle, roll yourself into one ball with it — walking thus, sitting thus, lying thus, not one half-second letting go; touch it in some chance meeting of circumstance and one thought answers — the present-day Pang Yun, Yang Danian, the Vice-Marshal, walking hand in hand. And Chaozong Tongren grades the pair: not taking the myriad dharmas as companion is already dragging mud and water; swallowing the West River still not wetting one drop — Pang forever carrying the board, tapped at ribs and chest; Mazu spending machine beyond the gauge, all releasing, all seizing; even swallowing the West River whole gives no place to stand, let alone guarding a no-companion state sitting on the hundred-foot pole. Yun'e Xi picks the case up and answers in Fengxue's stead: Old Pang had nowhere to find a mate, and Mazu's find is rarer still — to this very day, lonely, cold and quiet — but Fengxue would answer otherwise: who is the one who takes none of the myriad dharmas as companion? the grasses weep dew in a thousand ways, the pines hum one same song in the wind. Guxue Zhenzhe, after running the original — Mazu's blade playing round the ox entire, Pang reading autumn from one falling leaf, one pluck of the string another song — offers his own barter: if today someone asked Cuiyan this, he would only tell him: when you can push over the Five Old Peaks, then I will tell you. And Yezhu Fuhui, writing to a layman who wants to study the old man, retells it under Pang's courtesy name — Daoxuan asked Shitou, the hand came over the mouth, Daoxuan had a stir; then Mazu and the West River, and the sudden grasp of the purport — and rules: without Shitou's opening and Mazu's gauge-breaking tongs, this man would have been nothing but one more dresser and eater, what fame would reach today? so, would-be student, go swallow the whole river first.
